title: Controversial Reception of 'The Last Photograph' at TIFF
seoTitle: Controversial Reception of 'The Last Photograph' at TIFF
subtitle: Zack Snyder's new film, 'The Last Photograph', premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and is already sparking strong reactions among critics and fans.
excerpt: Zack Snyder's new independent project, 'The Last Photograph', is trending in searches after its debut at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The new project by filmmaker Zack Snyder, titled The Last Photograph, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), generating a wave of searches and online debates. The film's screening at the festival was accompanied by a flood of negative reviews, reigniting discussion about the director's work and cinematic style.

What is 'The Last Photograph'?

The Last Photograph is a film Snyder describes as a personal project, the result of a 20‑year journey. The feature is an independent production, without the backing of major studios or streaming platforms, and was made on a budget smaller than some of the commercial movies Snyder directed early in his career. The story is set in an unnamed South American country and follows a war photographer and the brother of an assassinated diplomat, who team up on a jungle trek to find the family's kidnapped children. Snyder calls it a “meditation on death and redemption” and on “how people see the world in different ways.”

Zack Snyder's new approach

For this film, Snyder served as director and cameraman, a role he performed in his early commercial work. The production of The Last Photograph departed from the hallmarks of his big‑budget movies: there is no green screen, nor any slow‑motion. His wife and producing partner, Deborah Snyder, noted that the project “almost harks back to his roots in commercials and music videos,” with a smaller crew and striking visuals without the need for “bells and whistles.” Snyder acquired the rights to The Last Photograph from Warner Bros. and cast Stuart Martin and Fra Fee, both actors from his film Rebel Moon, in the lead roles. The movie also features a score co‑composed by Hans Zimmer.

Behind the scenes in Colombia

Filming for The Last Photograph took place in southern Colombia, including the city of Leticia on the banks of the Amazon River. Snyder faced challenging conditions during production, shooting in three‑digit heat and contracting COVID, with a fever also in the three‑digit range. He described the experience as “unique and intimate,” noting that the shoot lasted 32 days, the shortest of any film he has made. Snyder reported averaging 40 camera setups per day, reaching 72 on a single shooting day, compared with the four setups he sometimes used on productions like Justice League.

Reception from critics and fans

The debut of The Last Photograph at TIFF provoked a strong reaction from critics. Posts on X (formerly Twitter) cited reviews ranging from “Worst film of Zack’s career” to “A tedious, frustrating, exhausting experience.” Comments such as “Uh oh, another Zack Snyder whiff on the way!” were frequent. This negative reception adds to earlier criticism of Snyder’s projects, like Rebel Moon. However, the director’s fan base rallied in defense of the film, with statements like “If the so‑called critics didn’t like Zack Snyder’s movie, that means the movie will be great.” The polarized opinions highlighted a split among Snyder’s admirers.

Snyder and the future of cinema

Reflecting on his career and the current film landscape, Snyder compared the success of Marvel movies, which he sees as “a theme‑park ride,” with his own interest in the “mythology” of characters. He admitted that this approach might not be “that fun,” but he can’t work any other way. Looking ahead, Snyder is already planning a remake of John Carpenter’s classic Escape from New York, set in 1997. He also mentioned a return to Warner Bros. for a special screening of a film, but noted he hasn’t yet seen recent DC movies such as James Gunn’s Superman, although he supports the division’s success.

With information from The Hollywood Reporter, Yardbarker.
